newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: WTO infotech deal seen spurring investment in Asia.
newsitem.headline: WTO infotech deal seen spurring investment in Asia.

text.p: A global deal to scrap tariffs on information technology products from chips to computers will likely spur a shift of investment from Europe to Asia and benefit big corporate players who already dominate key market sectors, analysts say.

The European Union said on Thursday it had agreed with the United States to scrap tariffs on billions of dollars worth of infotech products by 2000, clearing the way for a broader global deal with Japan, Canada and key developing nations.

Trade ministers from the 128-member World Trade Organisation (WTO) have been struggling at their meeting in Singapore this week to clinch a pact to eliminate tariffs on some 180 products in the fast-growing infotech sector, estimated now to be worth some $600 billion annually, by the year 2000.

Negotiators from the Big Four trade partners -- the United States, Japan, the European Union and Canada -- had been at odds over key issues such as product coverage even as they sought to persuade other WTO members including key Asian nations to join in the proposed Information Technology Agreement (ITA).
A senior Japanese trade official said Big Four disputes over product coverage had nearly all been settled, although some gaps still remained between Japan and the EU.

Washington has been the loudest cheerleader for an infotech deal and the hordes of U.S. corporate lobbyists on the fringes of the WTO conference reflected private-sector expectations that a deal would boost profits.

U.S. officials have touted the deal as a huge plus for American corporate profits. "The ITA opens up markets that are at the core of U.S. competitiveness, expanding opportunities for America's world-class producers of software and semiconductors, computers and telecommunications equipment," the U.S. Trade Reprentative's office said last month after Asian-Pacific leaders broadly endorsed an infotech deal.
Analysts agreed that U.S. firms' lead in key infotech sectors meant that such companies would see big benefits.
"It is only natural that America is keen, given their strong position in personal computers, software and cellular phones," said an analyst at a foreign brokerage in Tokyo.
Japan -- whose tariffs on many infotech products are already at or close to zero -- has also been keen to see an infotech pact forged.
Together, Japan and the United States account for over one-third of infotech exports, according to WTO data.
"There is no downside to an infotech pact for Japan," the analyst said.

But the European Union's relatively higher tariffs mean Brussels stands to lose most, both in terms of protection for domestic industry and incentives for foreign firms to invest inside Europe so as to get around tariff barriers -- a fact clearly reflected in EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan's tough negotiating stance at intense talks here this week.

The United States and Canada have already pledged to cut tariffs on key infotech products to under nine percent by 1999 under the Uruguay Round of world trade talks, but the EU's Uruguay Round pledges would have left tariffs as high as 14 percent on some goods, Japanese Trade Ministry data shows.
Tariff elimination means multinational firms keen to take advantage of lower Asian labour costs will have good cause to shift investment and output to Asia, analysts said.

"There will be less incentive to come in (to Europe) to make products locally. They will increase investment in Asia, where labour is cheaper, and export to Europe," said David Benda, industry analyst at BZW Securities in Tokyo.
"It may well be that Europe will lose out," he said.

Besides the Big Four trade powers, some 30 countries including key players in the dynamic Asia-Pacific markets, are expected to join the infotech pact initially -- although some want flexibility over the timing and final implementation of the tariff elimination, a Japanese official said.

Scrapping tariffs, however, is unlikely to result in big shifts in corporate market share in the infotech sector, BZW's Benda said. "If tariffs fall, companies which already have a share in any given category will see sales improve, but the increase will be proportional (to that share)," he said.
"After all, tariffs apply to everyone," he said.
